title: A pattern across living conditions

blocks.heading: A pattern across living conditions
blocks.text: Higher development is commonly associated with higher income per person, longer life expectancy and wider education and health access. Adequate housing includes shelter and access to essential services; diet concerns sufficient and varied food as well as the ability to buy it. Job opportunities matter through earnings, stability, safety and skills. A change from agriculture towards industrial and service employment can accompany development, but the sector name alone says little about wages or working conditions. Population growth also varies. It should be described from the source, rather than assumed from a country label.

blocks.heading: A fictional comparison
blocks.text: In a same-year synthetic table, Country K has annual income per person of N$22,000, life expectancy of 61 years and 58% of households with a basic sanitation service. Country L has N$68,000, 76 years and 91%. L combines higher income with longer life expectancy and wider sanitation access. The income difference is N$46,000, life expectancy is 15 years longer and sanitation access is 33 percentage points higher. The pattern spans economic and social conditions. It does not describe income inequality within either country. Nor does it justify a stereotype about an individual resident's diet, occupation or health.

blocks.heading: Describe people as well as production
blocks.text: Population in Topic 7.1, health in Topic 7.2 and education in Topic 7.3 provide explanations for these patterns. Start with what a table shows, select the relevant features, and distinguish a general association from a claim about every person. A useful comparison links the same characteristic across the two places.
